one_liner: Nim HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket server with built-in TLS; about 30% more req/s than actix-web on an empty GET /.
what_it_does: Caprese is a Nim macro DSL that compiles a whole web server into one self-contained executable: a `config:` block, then `server(ip, port):` / `routes(host):` blocks with `get "/path":` handlers that build a response string with `addHeader()` and `send` it. Built in: WebSocket `stream:` blocks, a prefix-match reverse proxy (TCP or UNIX socket), static files embedded at compile time with precompressed Brotli/Deflate variants, SNI multi-certificate TLS with Let's Encrypt certificate hot-reload, an IP filter, and tag-based fan-out of messages to WebSocket clients. It is not a drop-in for actix-web: it is a different language, and the API is compile-time macros, not a handler/extractor library.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker thread (one per CPU by default) runs epoll_wait on one shared edge-triggered epoll set (kqueue on OpenBSD). The listening socket is registered with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, clients come from a preallocated pool, and each client has its own spinlock. The request parser extracts only the headers declared at compile time (`httpHeader:` plus a few internal ones). It uses macro-generated 8-byte and 4-byte word compares (`cmpString`, and `cmpHeaderParam` with OR-0x20 case folding) and a computed-goto case per target header, and it stops scanning once every wanted header is found. With `activeHeader = true`, as in the benchmark app, a response built from a static string is a precomputed byte buffer (status line, headers, body); a background thread patches the Date field once per second into a double buffer.
when_to_use: A Linux (or OpenBSD) service in Nim that pushes real-time messages to many WebSocket clients, especially fan-out by tag (for example, notifying every wallet that watches an address), which is the use case it was built for.

A small, fixed set of GET endpoints that return static or precomputed bodies over keep-alive, where throughput and median latency matter more than tail latency (median 2.17 ms vs actix-web 3.13 ms at c=512 in the benchmark run).

You want one statically linked binary that terminates TLS itself (BearSSL, OpenSSL, LibreSSL or BoringSSL chosen at compile time), does SNI, reloads Let's Encrypt certificates without a restart, embeds its static assets, and proxies a few paths to back ends, with no nginx in front.
Full-stack Nim projects that also generate their HTML (Karax) and minified JavaScript (Nim JS backend plus closure-compiler) in the same code base and binary.
when_not_to_use: Tail-latency-sensitive services: in the same run caprese's p99 was 10.6 ms vs actix-web 3.2 ms at c=512 and 6.6 ms vs 0.39 ms at c=64, so the throughput lead came with much more jitter.

General REST APIs: routing is GET-centric. POST is off by default, and enabling it prints the compile warning 'POST is not yet implemented.'; streamed large request bodies are not implemented, there are no PUT/DELETE/HEAD route helpers in the README, and Transfer-Encoding parsing is commented out. HTTP/2, QUIC, IPv6 and cookies are listed as not done.

macOS or Windows: only Linux and OpenBSD are supported. `nimble install` fails on macOS with "attempting to call undeclared routine: 'accept4'" (issue #2, open since 2024-12), and the maintainer puts Windows support 'a few years later' (issue #1).

Teams that need an ecosystem, middleware, API docs beyond one README, or versioned releases: the package has been version 0.1.0 with no tags or releases, has one maintainer, 84 stars and no pull requests.

Reproducible or audited builds: the nimble build hook runs `git submodule update --init --remote`, so it compiles the latest upstream HEADs of BearSSL, OpenSSL, LibreSSL, BoringSSL, Brotli and zopfli unless you set NOREMOTEUPDATE=1.

integration.form: module (nimble package; macros expand into your program; TLS, Brotli and zopfli C libraries are built from git submodules and statically linked)
integration.dependencies: Nim packages karax >= 1.2.3, regex, checksums; C libraries built from submodules: BearSSL, OpenSSL, LibreSSL, BoringSSL (all four are built unless NOSSL=1), Brotli, zopfli; the build needs git, automake, autoconf, libtool and cmake; Java and Maven only if you use the closure-compiler JavaScript minifier
integration.min_toolchain: Nim >= 1.6.4 per caprese.nimble, with --threads:on (compile error otherwise); README builds use --mm:orc; the benchmark used Nim 2.2
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll; Debian/Ubuntu recommended) and OpenBSD (kqueue); macOS build fails; no Windows. CPU architecture is not documented; the word-compare parser code reads 8-byte words, so 64-bit targets are implied
integration.thread_safety: Route bodies run concurrently on serverWorkerNum threads (default: CPU count) and must return immediately; blocking work goes through a `Pendings` queue to `worker(num)` threads, which reply by ClientId. Some Client methods may only be called from route (dispatch-level) code, and using `getClient(ClientId)` from workers needs your own locking (README).

gotchas: The benchmarked configuration is not the default: the-benchmarker app sets sslLib = None, activeHeader = true and connectionPreferred = InternalConnection, while the defaults are BearSSL, activeHeader = false and ExternalConnection (a different, throttled dispatch path). activeHeader only precomputes responses whose body is a compile-time static string.
By default responses carry no Date or Server header (headerDate and headerServer default to false); enable headerDate if clients or caches expect one.

Only headers declared in `httpHeader:` are parsed, and `reqHeader()` works only inside `routes:` because values point into the receive buffer. The request parser accepts only request lines that start with 'GET /' (POST, when enabled, takes a separate path); HEAD, PUT, DELETE or OPTIONS requests get a parse error.
connectionTimeout (default 120 s) is approximate: the README says disconnection happens between the set time and twice that time. clientMax (default 32000) client slots are preallocated at start-up.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over httpbeast, the other Nim entry: caprese did 212.6k vs 175.5k req/s at c=512 with similar p99 (10.6 vs 11.3 ms) and adds TLS, WebSocket and a proxy, so in Nim it is the faster choice. may_minihttp and fulmine.js were within 4-9% of caprese's throughput at c=512 with about 4x lower p99 (2.7-2.8 ms); pick them unless you are in Nim or need caprese's built-in TLS and WebSocket fan-out.
verified_claims_summary: In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (commit f673364; GET / with an empty text body over keep-alive, zrk closed loop, mean of 3 runs), caprese 0.1 built with Nim 2.2 without TLS (-d:release --opt:speed plus -flto, per the Nim Dockerfile) did 233,622 / 222,921 / 212,564 req/s at c=64/256/512 against actix-web 4.8's 179,203 / 168,270 / 163,415 (30-32% more), and it was first of all frameworks at each level. Both servers used about 3.95 cores in Docker on one 16-vCPU x86_64 host whose CPU name reads 'M1 Eight-Core Processor'. Caprese sent about 118 bytes per response vs actix-web's 88, so the lead is not from a smaller response; its median latency was lower but its p99 was 3.3x higher at c=512.
status_note: Active single-maintainer project (near-daily commits up to 2026-08-04, recently on an experimental `server2` engine) but still version 0.1.0 with no tags or releases, so pin a git commit; MIT-licensed, and the core `server.nim` is a single 6,400-line file.
